title: Who can open your link: sharing files safely

narration: Imagine you send a budget link to three teammates.
A week later, a stranger is reading it.
beats.visual_intent: A drawn budget document with three teammate pictograms beside it, then a fourth figure in an empty box with a question mark appears reading it

grounding.claim: Illustration: a link sent to three people reaches an unintended reader

narration: How did it get there?
Nobody hacked anything.
The link simply travelled.
beats.visual_intent: A hand-drawn line carries the link from one teammate to a second figure and on to the stranger, passing the sender by

grounding.claim: A forwarded link can be opened by a new holder without the sender being asked; this is not hacking

narration: Three quick choices stop that.
Who can open it.
What they can do.
And until when.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter introduces three choices; three short written words appear on the board beside her, one per spoken phrase

grounding.claim: Promise built on the least-privilege checks: who, what, and when access ends

narration: You paste links like this every week.
Think of one as a key.
A key opens for whoever holds it.
beats.visual_intent: A document drawn as a door with a rough key beside it; the key is drawn, then a hand-off arrow shows it passing to another holder

grounding.claim: Framing metaphor only: on broad settings the link itself grants access to whoever holds it

narration: First key: anyone with the link.
Whoever holds it can open the file.
In many tools, no sign-in needed.
beats.visual_intent: The widest of three rough rings drawn around the document, a crowd of pictograms inside it, the label written beside the ring

grounding.claim: Anyone with the link can open the document, and in many tools need not sign in

narration: Second: people in the company.
Anyone signed in, not just your team.
Outsiders stay out.
beats.visual_intent: A middle ring drawn inside the first holding many company pictograms, outsiders left outside it; the label written beside the ring

grounding.claim: The company-wide setting works for people signed in to the organisation, not for people outside it

narration: Third: named people.
Here the door checks you, not just the key.
Only accounts you added get in.
beats.visual_intent: A small inner ring holding three named pictograms; the door checks each person's face against a list, the one place the key analogy breaks

grounding.claim: Named people opens only for the specific accounts added, each signed in as that account

narration: Widest to narrowest, in that order.
Pick the narrowest that works.
Your company may set rules too. Check.
beats.visual_intent: The three rings shown together with an arrow from widest to narrowest and the pocket rule written under them, then a small note about company rules

grounding.claim: The settings run widest to narrowest; choose the narrowest that works
Organisations may set their own rules or defaults

narration: Now, what can they do inside?
With view, they read the budget.
They cannot change your original.
beats.visual_intent: The budget page drawn with an eye icon beside it; a hand reaches in and the original page stays unchanged

grounding.claim: With view access a holder can read but not change the original

narration: Edit is different.
Holders can change the original.
Everyone sees the change.
beats.visual_intent: A pencil marks a figure on the budget page, and the same change appears on every holder's copy of the page

grounding.claim: With edit access a holder can change the original and everyone sees the changes

narration: Here is where people slip.
View protects the original.
Depending on the tool, it may not stop copying.
beats.visual_intent: The viewing eye icon, then a hand copying the page text to a second sheet, with a written note that it depends on the tool

grounding.claim: A viewer may still be able to copy or download content, depending on tool and settings

narration: So for the budget, start with view.
Edit only when they must change it.
Keep those three doors in mind.
beats.visual_intent: A tick beside view, edit written with a small question mark; the three rings from before return faintly behind

recall.prompt: Keep the three doors in mind: anyone with the link, people in the company, named people.

grounding.claim: Give view access unless the person needs to edit

narration: Here is the tricky part.
Say the link is set to the company.
A teammate forwards it to a manager elsewhere.
beats.visual_intent: The company ring on the board with the three teammates inside; a line leaves one teammate and reaches a new figure elsewhere in the ring

grounding.claim: Illustration: a company-wide link forwarded once to another colleague

narration: She opens it. Nobody asks you.
The link itself is the permission.
It can travel on, but only inside the company.
beats.visual_intent: The manager's figure opens the page, a second forward arrow leaves her and stops at the edge of the company ring, an outsider figure turned back

grounding.claim: On broad settings the link grants access to a new holder without asking the sender, who can forward it again; company-wide stays limited to signed-in company accounts
The link itself grants access on broad settings

narration: Anyone with the link has no such edge.
on_screen: Anyone with the link: no edge
beats.visual_intent: The same forward arrow on the widest ring continues past where the company edge was, off toward the board's border

grounding.claim: On the anyone setting whoever holds the link can open it however they got it

narration: Same forward, but the link is set to named people.
The door asks who she is.
Where the list is enforced, it stays shut.
beats.visual_intent: The forward arrow reaches the inner door; a rough list of three names is checked against the manager and the door stays closed with a cross marker

grounding.claim: With named people a forwarded link does not open for someone not on the list, where the tool enforces it

narration: A listed person could still show it on.
So choose names you trust.
The link travels. A name does not.
beats.visual_intent: A listed figure shows the page over a shoulder in a small note, then the two written lines sit under the board as the pocket rule

grounding.claim: A listed person can still show or copy the content to others

narration: Your turn.
Say three teammates need to read the budget,
not change it.
Which setting, and which permission?
Pause, and decide.
beats.visual_intent: A quiz card with three options, each pairing a setting with a permission, and no answer shown

recall.question: Say three teammates need to read the budget, not change it. Which setting, and which permission?
recall.why: It is the narrowest setting that works, and view is enough to read.
recall.tempting_wrong: People in the company, view: one forward would open it to everyone signed in to the company.

grounding.claim: Illustration: three teammates who only need to read a budget draft
Quiz built on the narrowest-setting and view-first checks

narration: Named people, with view.
The company setting sounds close.
But one forward opens it to everyone signed in.
Named people holds it to three.
on_screen: Company: a forward reaches everyone signed in
beats.visual_intent: The answer card marks named people with view as right and fades the other two; the company option gets a written note about the forward

grounding.claim: Illustration: three teammates who only need to read a budget draft
Narrowest setting that works, view unless edit is needed
A forwarded company link reaches everyone signed in to the company
Named people holds the line against a forward

narration: Before you share, four quick checks.
Right file? Narrowest setting? View, unless edit?
And who is on the list?
beats.visual_intent: A checklist written down the board, one tick drawn beside each line as it is spoken

grounding.claim: Check the right file, the narrowest setting, view unless edit, and the access list
Check who is on the access list

narration: Then look inside the file.
Other pages, comments, version history.
Check, do not assume.
beats.visual_intent: The budget page drawn with a magnifier over it and three small tabs written beside it, one for each hidden place

grounding.claim: Check other pages, comments and version history for content that should not travel; visibility varies by tool

narration: Third choice: until when.
When the job is done, take the key back.
Switch it off, or narrow it, and remove names.
beats.visual_intent: The key drawn earlier is crossed out and returned to the sender's hand; a name on the list is struck through

grounding.claim: When access is no longer needed switch the link off or narrow it and remove named people who no longer need the file

narration: Many tools list what you have shared.
Review it, to find old links.
Some offer an expiry date, too.
beats.visual_intent: A rough list of three shared files with one old link ticked off, then a small calendar with a written end date

grounding.claim: Many tools list what you have shared, and reviewing finds old links still on
Some tools offer an expiry date on a link or on a person's access

narration: Back to the budget.
Named people, view only, switched off after.
A forwarded link now stops at the door.
beats.visual_intent: The opening board redrawn calmly: three named teammates inside the small ring, the forward arrow stopping at the closed door, the key returned

grounding.claim: Named people with view and later removal keeps a forwarded link from opening for others, where the tool enforces the list
Switch access off when done

narration: Before you press Share, ask three things.
Who could hold this?
Can they view it, or edit it?
When do I switch it off?
Narrowest door. View first. Switch off.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter beside three written questions on the board, then the pocket rule written as one line

grounding.claim: Transfer: the three questions follow the least-privilege checks and the end-of-access steps
Close access when no longer needed
